opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think if you look at where we are, there are really three big ingredients that got us here. There's the transformer and pre-training at scale, there's post-training, things like RLHF that make models actually useful and aligned with what people want, and then there's reasoning: training models with reinforcement learning to think for longer before they answer. Each of those was a genuine conceptual breakthrough, and each one took years to go from "this works in a research setting" to "this is a product hundreds of millions of people use."

When I look ahead, I don't see an obvious fourth missing piece. That isn't because I think research is over. There's an enormous amount of hard work left. But the work looks like scaling these ideas further, making them more efficient, and figuring out how to combine them well. Reasoning in particular is still very early. We've just started to see what happens when you scale up test-time compute and RL on harder and longer tasks.

There's also a historical perspective here. People have predicted a wall many times: we'd run out of data, scaling would stop working, models couldn't reason. Each time the field found a way through, and usually it wasn't some radically new paradigm. It was taking an existing idea seriously and pushing it much harder than people thought was reasonable.

So my bet is that if you showed someone from 2030 our current set of techniques, they'd recognize all the core concepts. What they'd find surprising is how much more compute, data, engineering, and refinement went into them. The frontier will be driven less by a eureka moment and more by relentless execution: better infrastructure, better data, better evals, and longer-horizon tasks. That's less romantic, but I think it's where the progress will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look back at the history of the field, there have really been three big ideas that got us here. The first was transformers, which gave us a general-purpose architecture that could scale. The second was scaling itself, the realization that if you just make these models bigger, train them on more data with more compute, you get predictably better results, and that pre-training on the internet gives you this enormous reservoir of knowledge about the world. And the third, which is more recent, is reasoning, teaching models to think before they answer, to spend compute at test time working through a problem instead of just blurting out the first thing that comes to mind.

And my view is that those three things, taken together, are enough. When I was at OpenAI, each of those felt like a genuine discovery, a moment where the field saw something it hadn't seen before. But I don't think we need a fourth one of that magnitude to get to something that looks like AGI. What's left is mostly execution. It's engineering. It's building out the compute, figuring out how to make reasoning work across more domains, extending models from answering questions to actually doing long, multistep tasks as agents. That's hard work, and it'll take years, but it's the kind of hard work where you know roughly what the path looks like.

The reason I believe this is that nothing I've seen in the last couple of years has required a new paradigm to explain it. Every time people said the models would plateau, the plateau turned out to be a scaling problem or a data problem, not a conceptual one. So the honest prediction is that the next several years look like the last several, just with much more capable systems coming out of the same basic recipe.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest evidence is that we keep getting more capable systems by scaling up essentially the same methods. We give them more compute, more data, and better training, and they develop abilities that we didn’t explicitly build into them. That suggests the methods are doing something fairly general, rather than solving one narrow problem at a time.

That doesn’t mean there are no discoveries left to make. There’s an enormous amount we still don’t understand. But I distinguish between needing a new fundamental idea and needing to figure out how to make the ideas we have work really well. My bet is that a lot of what stands between us and much greater intelligence is in that second category.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that we’ve found a surprisingly general recipe: train a large neural network to predict data, and it learns much more than we initially expected. To predict language well, for example, it helps to learn something about the world, about people’s intentions, and about how to reason through a problem.

And we keep seeing that as we give these systems more compute, more data, and better training, they become more capable. We haven’t yet seen clear evidence that this approach hits a fundamental ceiling.

That doesn’t mean there are no discoveries left. There’s a huge amount of work in figuring out how to train these systems efficiently, how to let them learn from their mistakes, and how to make them reliable. But those may be advances within the basic framework we already have, rather than requiring an entirely new idea about intelligence. I think that’s a plausible bet, though certainly not something we know for sure.
